title: Passion, Resurrection and the Historical Jesus
bigQuestion: When four accounts of the same days differ, what can a reader learn from the differences, and what can a historian say about the man behind them?

story.title: Four Columns on One Table
story.kicker: A class lays the last chapters of four gospels side by side and starts counting what matches and what does not.
paragraphs: The teacher hands out four photocopies and a highlighter. Each sheet holds the story of one Friday: Mark 14–15, Matthew 26–27, Luke 22–23, John 18–19. The students tape them to the table in four columns, in the order most scholars think they were written, Mark first. The task is simple. Highlight every sentence that appears in all four. Then mark what appears in only one.

The columns fill with color fast. A supper. A garden. An arrest at night. A hearing before the high priest, then a hearing before Pilate, the Roman governor. A crowd. A man named Barabbas released. A cross outside the city, two others crucified alongside, a sign over the head, a burial before sundown. All four have these. The order is almost the same. The students expected more disagreement than this.

Then the single-column marks begin. Only Luke sends Jesus to King Herod for a hearing. Only Matthew tells of Pilate's wife's dream and Pilate washing his hands. Only John records a long conversation between Jesus and Pilate that ends with the governor asking, "What is truth?" The last words from the cross differ: Mark and Matthew give one saying, Luke three different ones, John three others. The sign over the cross is worded four ways.

A student asks the obvious question. Which one is right? The teacher answers with another question. Right about what? If the question is what a Roman execution looked like, historians can say a good deal. If the question is what the death of Jesus means, that is what each gospel is answering, and each answers in its own way. A reader can hold both questions at once, as long as she knows which one she is asking.

This chapter does what the class did. It reads the four Passion narratives together, then the accounts of the empty tomb and the resurrection, which Christians hold as the center of their faith. It then turns to the historian's question: what can be known about Jesus of Nazareth from sources inside and outside the New Testament? Finally it looks at how Jews and Muslims have understood Jesus, and how a person can study a text that others, or they themselves, believe.
story.think: The four accounts agree on the order of events and differ in details and sayings. What kinds of questions would the agreement help answer, and what kinds would the differences help answer?

lessons.title: Reading in Four Columns
lessons.mainIdea: The Passion narratives are the longest continuous stories in the gospels, and reading them side by side is the standard method for seeing what each writer chose.
reading: The *Passion* is the Christian name for the suffering and death of Jesus, from the Latin word for suffering. Each gospel devotes about two chapters to the last day, far more space than to any other single day. Many scholars think the Passion narrative was the first part of the Jesus story to be told as a connected account, before the gospels were written, because the four agree so closely on its order. The rest of each gospel is arranged more freely.

The four gospels are not four independent reports. Most scholars date Mark first, around 70 CE, and think Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source, adding material of their own. These three are called the *Synoptic Gospels*, from a Greek word meaning seen together, because they can be laid in parallel columns. John, usually dated around 90 to 100 CE, tells the story in a different order with long speeches and few parables, and many scholars think it was written without direct use of the other three.

None of the gospels names its author in the text. The names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John come from titles attached in the second century, and church tradition identifies them with two apostles and two companions of apostles. Many scholars treat the authors as unknown early Christians writing for particular communities. This course uses the traditional names as labels for the books, as scholars of all views do.

Reading in columns has a name: *redaction criticism*, the study of how each editor, or redactor, shaped shared material. When Matthew keeps a scene from Mark but adds a line, or Luke drops one, the change is evidence of that writer's concerns. The method does not tell a reader what happened. It shows what each gospel wants its reader to see, which is a different and answerable question.

words.d: the suffering and death of Jesus as the gospels tell it; from the Latin for suffering
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share so much material that they can be seen together in parallel columns
the study of how each gospel writer edited and arranged shared material to express his own concerns

look.title: When the Gospels Were Written
look.cite: Midpoints of the ranges most scholars give (Mark c. 65–75; Matthew and Luke c. 80–90; John c. 90–100); some scholars date all four earlier
look.prompt: If Mark was written about forty years after the crucifixion, what kinds of sources might its writer have used? What does the gap suggest about how the story was carried before then?

check.q: Which three gospels are called the Synoptic Gospels?
check.why: Matthew, Mark and Luke share so much material that they can be seen together. John stands apart in order and style.

check.q: Which gospel do most scholars think was written first?
check.why: Most scholars date Mark to about 70 CE and think Matthew and Luke used it as a source.

check.q: What does redaction criticism study?
choices: The Greek grammar of the gospels
The ages of the surviving manuscripts
How each gospel writer edited and arranged shared material
Whether the events of the Passion happened
check.why: Redaction criticism compares the gospels to see each writer's choices. It describes the editing, not the historicity, of the events.

lessons.title: The Night in the Garden
lessons.mainIdea: The Gethsemane scene shows Jesus in distress in Mark and calm in John, and the difference is a window on how each gospel presents him.
reading: After the last supper, the Synoptic Gospels take Jesus and his disciples to a place called *Gethsemane*, an olive grove on the Mount of Olives across the valley from Jerusalem. Mark 14:32–42 describes him as deeply distressed. He asks three disciples to stay awake, goes a little farther, falls to the ground and prays that the hour might pass. The prayer begins with the Aramaic word *Abba*, father. He asks to be spared the cup, an image from the prophets for suffering, and then submits: not what I will, but what you will. The disciples fall asleep three times.

Matthew 26 follows Mark closely. Luke 22 shortens the scene to a single prayer, adds an angel who strengthens him, and describes sweat falling like drops of blood. Those two verses, Luke 22:43–44, are missing from several of the oldest manuscripts, and scholars are divided about whether Luke wrote them. Most modern translations print them with a note. It is one of several places in the Passion story where the manuscripts themselves are part of the question.

John tells it differently. John 18 has Jesus enter a garden across the Kidron valley, but there is no anguished prayer. Instead, when the soldiers come, Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek, and when he says "I am he" they fall to the ground. Earlier, in John 12:27, Jesus says his soul is troubled but refuses to ask to be saved from the hour. John's Jesus knows what will happen and goes to meet it. Readers have long noticed that John presents Jesus's divine identity more openly than the Synoptics do.

Christians have read Gethsemane as showing that Jesus was fully human and fully willing. Historians reading by the *criterion of embarrassment*, the principle that a community is unlikely to invent a story that makes its hero look weak, tend to regard the distress in Mark as an early tradition. Both readings are responses to the same text; a careful student can state each without confusing them.

words.d: an olive grove on the Mount of Olives where the Synoptic Gospels place Jesus's prayer and arrest
the Aramaic word for father, used in Mark 14:36
a historian's rule that a tradition unflattering to its hero is unlikely to have been invented

look.title: The Prayer in Mark
look.text: Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt.
look.prompt: The prayer asks for one thing and then accepts another. Compare it with John 12:27, where Jesus refuses to ask to be saved from the hour. What does each gospel want the reader to see about Jesus?

check.q: Which gospel has no anguished prayer in the garden and shows Jesus stepping forward to meet the soldiers?
check.why: John 18 has the arrest in a garden but no prayer of distress. Mark, Matthew and Luke all include the prayer.

check.q: Why do modern translations print Luke 22:43–44, the angel and the sweat like blood, with a note?
choices: The verses are missing from several of the oldest manuscripts
The verses are written in Latin
The King James Version omits them
check.why: Several early manuscripts lack the verses, so scholars are unsure whether Luke wrote them. The KJV includes them.

check.q: What does the criterion of embarrassment suggest about the Gethsemane distress in Mark?
choices: It was invented to make Jesus seem divine
It is likely an early tradition, since it makes the hero look weak
It proves the prayer's exact words
check.why: Historians reason that a community would be unlikely to invent a scene unflattering to its hero. The criterion suggests an early tradition; it does not prove exact wording.

lessons.title: Two Trials and a Question
lessons.mainIdea: The gospels place Jesus before Jewish leaders and then before Pilate, and the way each gospel divides responsibility has had serious consequences for Jews in later centuries.
reading: All four gospels describe a hearing before the high priest, Caiaphas. Then comes a hearing before *Pontius Pilate*, the Roman governor of Judea from about 26 to 36 CE. Only Rome could carry out a crucifixion. The charge Pilate acts on is political: king of the Jews. Mark 14 describes a night session of the council, the *Sanhedrin*. Witnesses disagree, and the session ends in a charge of blasphemy. Luke places the council meeting in the morning and adds a hearing before Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. John has no council trial at all, only questioning by the former high priest Annas.

The Pilate scenes grow longer from gospel to gospel. Mark's Pilate asks a few questions and gives way to the crowd. Matthew adds Pilate's wife's dream. Matthew's Pilate also washes his hands and says he is innocent of this man's blood. John gives a long exchange. Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world. Pilate asks, "What is truth?" and leaves without waiting for an answer. Each gospel, in its own way, shows Pilate reluctant and the local leaders and crowd pressing for death.

Here the text has a history that must be told. Matthew 27:25 has the crowd say, "His blood be on us, and on our children." For centuries some Christians read that verse as a curse on all Jews for all time. They used the charge of deicide, killing God, to justify persecution. Historians answer on three points. Roman governors, not crowds, ordered crucifixions. The Jewish writers Philo and Josephus describe Pilate as harsh, not hesitant. And the gospels were written when Christians were separating from other Jews and living under Rome, which shaped how blame was assigned.

In 1965 the Catholic Church's declaration Nostra Aetate addressed this. It stated that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today. Many Protestant bodies have issued similar statements. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine have worked with Christian scholars on reading these chapters. A student reading the trials should hold three things at once: what each text says, what historians think happened, and what the text has been used to do.

words.d: the Roman governor of Judea from about 26 to 36 CE, who in all four gospels orders the crucifixion
the council of Jewish leaders in Jerusalem; the Synoptic Gospels describe it questioning Jesus
the killing of God; a charge some Christians once laid against Jews, rejected by the Catholic Church in 1965
the 1965 Vatican declaration that rejected blaming Jews as a people for the death of Jesus

look.title: Pilate's Question
look.text: Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault at all.
look.prompt: Pilate asks a question and leaves without an answer. What does John gain by letting the Roman governor voice that question? How would the scene read if Pilate had waited?

check.q: Who alone had the authority to carry out a crucifixion in Judea?
check.why: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment ordered by Roman authority. That is why the gospels have Pilate give the sentence.

check.q: Which gospel adds a hearing before Herod Antipas?
check.why: Luke 23:6–12 sends Jesus to Herod, ruler of Galilee. No other gospel includes it.

check.q: What did Nostra Aetate (1965) declare about the Passion?
choices: That Pilate was innocent of any wrongdoing
That the death of Jesus cannot be charged against all Jews then living or Jews today
That Matthew 27:25 should be removed from the Bible
That the trials never took place
check.why: The Catholic declaration rejected collective blame of Jews for the crucifixion. It did not remove any verse or rule on Pilate.

lessons.title: The Cross and Its Sign
lessons.mainIdea: Crucifixion was a Roman public punishment, and the four accounts of it share a frame while differing in details such as the wording of the sign and the hour.
reading: *Crucifixion* was a Roman method of executing slaves, rebels and non-citizens. It was designed to be slow and public. The Jewish historian Josephus describes mass crucifixions during the war of 66–70 CE. In 1968 a heel bone pierced by an iron nail was found in a tomb near Jerusalem. It is the only physical remains of a crucified man found so far. The gospels say Jesus was flogged and made to carry the crossbeam. He was crucified at a place called Golgotha, skull, outside the city wall, with two others.

The shared frame is clear. A passerby named Simon of Cyrene carries the cross in the Synoptics. Soldiers divide the clothing, which the gospels connect with Psalm 22:18. A sign states the charge. Bystanders mock. In the Synoptics darkness falls from the sixth to the ninth hour. Jesus dies, and a Roman *centurion* speaks. Joseph of Arimathea buries the body before the Sabbath. Women who followed from Galilee watch, and Mary Magdalene is named in all four gospels.

The details differ. The sign reads "The King of the Jews" in Mark and "This is Jesus the King of the Jews" in Matthew. Luke has "This is the King of the Jews." John has "Jesus of Nazareth the King of the Jews," written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek. Mark 15:25 says the crucifixion began at the third hour, about nine in the morning. John 19:14 has Pilate still passing sentence at about the sixth hour, noon. Readers since ancient times have tried to reconcile the hours. Many modern scholars think each writer chose the time for its meaning. John's noon is when the Passover lambs were being killed.

Christians see the cross as the center of their faith: the death, they believe, by which God reconciles the world. Jewish tradition sees a Jewish man executed by Rome, one of thousands. Muslims, as the last section will show, generally believe he was not crucified at all. The historian says less and says it firmly. Crucifixion under Pilate is among the best-attested facts about Jesus. All four gospels report it, and so does the Roman writer Tacitus.

words.d: a Roman method of public execution by nailing or binding a person to a wooden cross
the place of the crucifixion outside Jerusalem's wall; the name means skull
a Roman army officer in charge of about eighty to a hundred soldiers

look.title: Four Signs, One Cross
look.text: Mark 15:26: The King of the Jews. Matthew 27:37: This is Jesus the King of the Jews. Luke 23:38: This is the King of the Jews. John 19:19: Jesus of Nazareth the King of the Jews, written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. All four agree on the charge. None agrees on the exact words.
look.prompt: If all four writers were copying one wooden sign, why might the wording differ? Which explanation fits best: memory, translation, each writer's purpose, or several at once?

check.q: Crucifixion was typically used by the Romans on which people?
check.why: Crucifixion was reserved for the low-status and the rebellious, which is why the charge on the sign is political: king of the Jews.

check.q: Which woman is named at the cross or tomb in all four gospels?
check.why: Mary Magdalene appears in all four Passion and resurrection accounts. Salome is named only in Mark.

check.q: How do Mark and John differ on the hour of the crucifixion?
choices: Mark says night; John says dawn
Mark says the third hour; John has Pilate still sentencing at the sixth
John says the third hour; Mark says the sixth
check.why: Mark 15:25 gives the third hour, about nine in the morning. John 19:14 has the sentence at about the sixth hour, noon.

sections.title: Last Words and an Empty Tomb

lessons.title: Seven Sayings in Three Sets
lessons.mainIdea: No gospel records all seven last words from the cross; Mark and Matthew give one, Luke three and John three, and each set fits its gospel's portrait of Jesus.
reading: Christians have traditionally counted seven *last words*, sayings of Jesus from the cross. Many churches read all seven together on Good Friday. But no single gospel has all seven. Mark and Matthew record one: a cry in Aramaic, translated as "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" It is the first line of Psalm 22. That psalm begins in abandonment and ends in praise. Readers disagree whether the cry is despair or a quotation that points to the psalm's hopeful ending.

Luke has three different sayings, and none is the cry of Psalm 22. Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." That verse is missing from some early manuscripts. He tells one of the men crucified beside him, who has asked to be remembered, that today he will be with him in paradise. He dies saying, "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit," from Psalm 31:5. Luke's Jesus dies as he lived in that gospel: forgiving, welcoming an outcast, and trusting.

John has three others. Jesus gives his mother into the care of the beloved disciple; he says, "I thirst," which John links to scripture; and his final word is "It is finished," a single Greek word meaning completed or accomplished. John's Jesus is in command to the end, as he was in the garden. The seven sayings, then, are three portraits laid over one another. Reading them separately, each in its own gospel, shows the portraits more sharply than reading them merged.

The same holds for the moment of death. In Mark the temple curtain tears and a centurion says, "Truly this man was the Son of God." Matthew adds an earthquake and tombs opening. Luke's centurion says, "Certainly this was a righteous man." John has a spear thrust and blood and water. A student who notices which detail belongs to which gospel is reading the way scholars read, and also the way careful believers have read since the early church.

words.d: the traditional seven sayings of Jesus from the cross, gathered from Mark and Matthew, Luke and John
a psalm beginning "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" that the Passion narratives quote and echo
the Friday before Easter, on which Christians remember the crucifixion

look.title: The Cry in Mark
look.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
look.prompt: Read the opening and closing verses of Psalm 22. Does quoting the first line invoke only despair, or the whole psalm? Give one argument for each reading.

check.q: Which gospels record the cry "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
check.why: Only Mark 15:34 and Matthew 27:46 record the cry from Psalm 22. Luke and John give different sayings.

check.q: Which last saying belongs to John?
choices: "Today you will be with me in paradise"
"Into thy hands I commend my spirit"
check.why: "It is finished" is John 19:30. The other three are Luke's sayings.

check.q: Why does the lesson suggest reading each gospel's last words separately rather than merged?
choices: Because merging them is forbidden by churches
Because each set fits its gospel's portrait of Jesus
Because the sayings contradict the Psalms
Because only Mark's saying is genuine
check.why: Luke's sayings show forgiveness and trust, John's command and completion. Reading them in their own gospels keeps the portraits distinct.

lessons.title: The Women at the Tomb
lessons.mainIdea: All four gospels say women found the tomb empty on the first day of the week, and Mark's oldest ending stops there, with the women afraid and silent.
reading: Each gospel says that early on the first day of the week, Sunday, women went to the tomb and found the stone rolled away and the body gone. Mark names Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. Matthew names two Marys. Luke names three women and others. John names Mary Magdalene alone, though she says "we" do not know where they have laid him. The number of women, the number of messengers at the tomb, one young man, one angel, two men, two angels, and what the women were told all vary.

Mark's account has a famous puzzle. The oldest and best manuscripts, including *Codex Sinaiticus* and Codex Vaticanus from the fourth century, end Mark at 16:8: the women flee from the tomb, trembling, and say nothing to anyone, because they are afraid. A longer ending, Mark 16:9–20, with appearances of the risen Jesus, is found in later manuscripts and in the King James Version. Nearly all scholars think it was added in the second century, and most modern Bibles mark it off. Whether Mark meant to end at 16:8, or his original ending was lost, is still debated.

Christians believe that the tomb was empty because Jesus rose from the dead, and Easter, the Sunday festival of the *resurrection*, is the oldest and central Christian holiday. Historians can say that belief in the resurrection arose very early; the apostle Paul, writing around 54 CE in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, quotes a list of appearances that he says he received, which most scholars date within a few years of the crucifixion. What a historian cannot do with historical tools is decide whether a resurrection occurred. That is a question of faith, and this course describes rather than decides it.

One detail draws comment from every kind of reader. In a culture where women's testimony carried little legal weight, all four gospels make women the first witnesses of the empty tomb. Christian apologists have argued the church would not have invented such witnesses. Some historians agree that the tradition is early; others note that the gospels also record women following Jesus throughout, so their presence at the tomb fits the story. Both note the same fact; they weigh it differently.

words.d: rising from the dead; Christians believe Jesus rose on the third day after his crucifixion
a fourth-century Greek manuscript of the Bible, found at St. Catherine's Monastery in the Sinai, that ends Mark at 16:8
the Sunday festival of the resurrection, the central holiday of the Christian year

look.title: Where the Oldest Manuscripts Stop
look.text: And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.
look.cite: Mark 16:8, King James Version (1611); Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus end the gospel here
look.prompt: If a book about good news ended with fear and silence, what might its writer be doing? Argue for one reading: the ending was lost, or the ending is deliberate.

check.q: Where do the oldest manuscripts of Mark end?
choices: At 16:8, with the women afraid and silent
check.why: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8. Verses 9–20 appear in later manuscripts and are widely thought to be a second-century addition.

check.q: Who is the first person named at the empty tomb in John's gospel?
check.why: John 20:1 names Mary Magdalene alone at the tomb. Peter arrives after she runs to tell him.

check.q: What can a historian say about the resurrection using historical tools?
choices: That it certainly did not happen
That belief in it arose very early, as Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 15 shows
Nothing at all, since no early source mentions it
check.why: Historians can date the belief early through 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 and the gospels. Whether the event occurred is a question of faith, outside historical method.

lessons.title: The Appearances and Their Settings
lessons.mainIdea: The gospels and Paul describe appearances of the risen Jesus in different places and to different people, and Christians hold them as the foundation of their faith.
reading: Matthew reports an appearance to the women near the tomb. Then comes one in *Galilee*, on a mountain, where Jesus sends the disciples to all nations. Luke keeps everything in and around *Jerusalem* on the same day. Two disciples walking to the village of Emmaus meet a stranger who explains the scriptures. They recognize him when he breaks bread. Then Jesus appears to the gathered disciples and eats fish. John has appearances in Jerusalem, including one to Thomas, who had doubted. John's final chapter is set by the Sea of Galilee.

The oldest written account is not in the gospels. Paul's first letter to the Corinthians is usually dated around 54 CE. It lists appearances to Peter, to the twelve, to more than five hundred at once, to James, to all the apostles, and last to Paul himself. Paul says he passed on what he had received. Most scholars think the list is a formula he learned when he joined the movement, within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul does not mention the empty tomb or the women. The gospels do not mention the five hundred.

Christians across traditions hold that these appearances were real encounters with a risen Jesus. The Nicene Creed, recited in Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches, says he rose on the third day. Within Christianity there are different views on whether the body was physically raised or transformed in some other way. The texts have been read to support both: Luke's Jesus eats fish, and John's passes through locked doors. Scholars who are not Christians describe the accounts as the earliest expressions of a belief that transformed a small Jewish movement.

The differences among the accounts have been studied for centuries. Harmonizers, from the second century on, have combined them into one sequence. Others, since the eighteenth century, have argued that the differences show the stories developing. A student needs neither verdict to do the basic work. Name each account, its date, its setting, its witnesses, and what it emphasizes. That is the work this whole unit has been practicing.

words.d: the northern region where Jesus grew up and taught; Matthew and John place resurrection appearances there
the city of the temple, the crucifixion and the tomb; Luke places all the appearances in and near it
a statement of Christian belief from 325 and 381 CE that affirms the resurrection on the third day

look.title: Who Saw Him, According to Paul
look.cite: 1 Corinthians 15:5–8, described from the King James Version (1611); "the twelve" is the group's name, though Judas is gone
look.prompt: Paul's list has no women and no empty tomb; the gospels have both. What might explain the different choices of a letter written about 54 CE and gospels written later?

check.q: Which gospel places all the resurrection appearances in and near Jerusalem on one day?
check.why: Luke 24 keeps everything around Jerusalem: Emmaus, the gathered disciples, and the parting. Matthew and John include Galilee.

check.q: What is the oldest written account of resurrection appearances?
check.why: 1 Corinthians is usually dated around 54 CE, before any gospel. The Creed is from the fourth century, and Mark's long ending is later than Mark.

check.q: Which appearance is found in Paul's list but in none of the gospels?
choices: To more than five hundred at once
check.why: Only Paul mentions the five hundred. The other three appearances are in the gospels and not in Paul.

lessons.title: Witnesses Outside the Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: Two non-Christian writers, Josephus and Tacitus, mention Jesus within about ninety years of his death, and both confirm the outline of a Jewish teacher executed under Pilate.
reading: *Josephus* was a Jewish general who surrendered to Rome in the war of 66–70 CE. He then wrote histories in Greek for Roman readers. His Jewish Antiquities, finished about 93 CE, mentions Jesus twice. The shorter passage, in Book 20, describes the execution in 62 CE of James, "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ." Most scholars accept it as genuine. The longer passage, in Book 18, calls Jesus a wise man and says Pilate condemned him to the cross. It also includes statements of Christian belief that a Jewish writer would not have made. Most scholars think a Christian copyist expanded an original, shorter notice.

*Tacitus*, a Roman senator and historian, wrote in his Annals around 116 CE about the fire of Rome in 64 CE. He says the emperor Nero blamed a group the people called Christians. Their name, he explains, came from Christus, who was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius. Tacitus despised the movement and calls it a pernicious superstition. That makes his notice valuable to historians: he had no reason to invent its founder.

Other mentions are thinner. Pliny the Younger, governor in Asia Minor around 112 CE, describes Christians singing to Christ as to a god. Suetonius mentions disturbances in Rome over one Chrestus. Rabbinic texts from later centuries contain a few passages that some scholars connect with Jesus, but they are late, hostile and disputed, and this course does not rely on them. The Qur'an, from the seventh century, speaks of Jesus at length but as a religious text, not a historical record of the first century.

What do the outside sources give? Not much detail, but a firm frame: a man called Christ, a brother named James, followers called Christians, and an execution ordered by Pilate under Tiberius, who reigned from 14 to 37 CE. Almost no historian of the ancient world doubts that Jesus existed. The debates are about what he taught, what he intended, and how the gospels relate to him. For those, the gospels themselves, read critically, remain the main evidence.

words.d: a Jewish historian (c. 37 to c. 100 CE) whose Jewish Antiquities mentions Jesus and his brother James
a Roman historian whose Annals (c. 116 CE) records that Christus was executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius
Roman emperor from 14 to 37 CE, during whose reign Pilate governed Judea

look.title: A Roman Senator on the Christians
look.text: Tacitus writes that Nero, to shift blame for the fire, punished a group the crowd called Christians; their name came from Christus, who had been executed in the reign of Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate; the superstition, checked for a moment, broke out again in Judea and in Rome.
look.cite: Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. 116 CE), paraphrased from the Church and Brodribb translation (1876)
look.prompt: Tacitus is hostile to the Christians. Why might a historian trust a hostile source on the bare facts more than a friendly one? What could a hostile source still get wrong?

check.q: Which passage in Josephus do most scholars accept as genuine?
choices: The notice in Book 20 about James, the brother of Jesus called Christ
The full text of the longer passage in Book 18
A description of the empty tomb
A quotation of the Sermon on the Mount
check.why: The Book 20 notice about James is widely accepted. The longer Book 18 passage is thought to have been expanded by a Christian copyist. Josephus says nothing of the tomb or sermon.

check.q: What does Tacitus report about Christus?
choices: That he rose from the dead
That he was executed by Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius
That he was born in Bethlehem
That he founded a school in Rome
check.why: Annals 15.44 records the execution under Pilate and Tiberius, and nothing about Jesus's birth or teaching.

check.q: Why does the lesson call Tacitus's hostility useful to historians?
choices: Because hostile writers are always accurate
Because it shows Tacitus had read the gospels
Because a writer who despised the movement had no reason to invent its founder
Because Tacitus was himself a Christian
check.why: A hostile witness has no motive to invent what he reports. That makes the bare facts he gives more credible, though not every detail.

lessons.title: How Historians Weigh the Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: Historians use stated criteria to sort gospel traditions, and although they disagree on much, a short list of facts about Jesus commands wide agreement.
reading: The *quest for the historical Jesus* is the name for two centuries of scholarly effort to describe Jesus using the tools of history. It began in Germany in the late 1700s, was surveyed by Albert Schweitzer in 1906, and continues today in a phase often called the third quest, which pays special attention to Jesus's Jewish setting. Its practitioners include Christians, Jews and people of no religion, and they argue with each other constantly.

The tools are called *criteria*. Multiple attestation: a saying or event reported in independent sources, such as Mark, Q, John and Paul, is more likely early. Embarrassment: a tradition awkward for the early church, like Jesus being baptized by John, whose baptism was for repentance, is unlikely to be invented. Dissimilarity: a saying unlike both Judaism of the time and the later church may go back to Jesus, though critics note it makes Jesus a stranger to his own world. Coherence with a first-century Galilean setting. None of the criteria is a proof; each is a reason to lean one way.

Applied with care, the criteria yield a short list that most historians accept. Jesus was a Jew from Galilee, from Nazareth. He was baptized by John the Baptist. He gathered followers, including a group of twelve, taught in parables and sayings, spoke of the kingdom of God, was known as a healer, and caused a disturbance in the temple. He was crucified by order of Pontius Pilate around 30 CE, and his followers soon afterward proclaimed that he had been raised. E. P. Sanders, whose 1985 book Jesus and Judaism helped shape the third quest, listed facts much like these.

Beyond the list, portraits diverge: an end-time prophet, a wisdom teacher, a healer, a social reformer, a messiah in his own eyes or not. The divergence is not a failure of the method; it reflects the limits of the evidence and the questions each historian brings. A student of this unit can recognize the moves. When a writer says "Jesus must have," ask which criterion is at work and which text is being weighed.

words.d: the scholarly effort, since the late 1700s, to describe Jesus with the methods of history
the rules historians use to weigh gospel traditions: multiple attestation, embarrassment, dissimilarity, coherence
the criterion that a tradition found in independent sources is more likely to be early

look.title: Apply a Criterion
look.text: Tradition A: Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist, whose baptism was for the forgiveness of sins (Mark 1:4–9). Matthew adds that John at first refused, saying he needed to be baptized by Jesus (Matthew 3:14). Tradition B: at the age of twelve Jesus amazed the teachers in the temple (Luke 2:41–52), a story found only in Luke.
look.prompt: Which criterion applies to each tradition, and what does it suggest? Explain why Matthew's added line is itself evidence for the criterion of embarrassment.

check.q: What does the criterion of multiple attestation say?
choices: A saying repeated many times in one gospel is early
A tradition found in independent sources is more likely early
The most popular reading is the correct one
A saying must appear in all four gospels to count
check.why: Independent sources, such as Mark, Q, John and Paul, count; repetition within one book does not, and four-gospel attestation is not required.

check.q: Why is Jesus's baptism by John often cited as an example of the criterion of embarrassment?
choices: Because John was a Roman official
Because the story appears only in Luke
Because a baptism for repentance was awkward for a church that held Jesus sinless
check.why: The early church would be unlikely to invent a scene in which Jesus receives a baptism of repentance. Matthew's added line shows the awkwardness.

check.q: Which of these is on the short list most historians accept about Jesus?
choices: He was crucified by order of Pontius Pilate
He wrote the Gospel of Mark
He lived in Rome under Nero
check.why: Crucifixion under Pilate is attested by all four gospels and Tacitus. The gospels are anonymous, and Jesus lived in Galilee and Judea, not Rome or Egypt.

lessons.title: Jesus in Jewish Tradition
lessons.mainIdea: Judaism does not regard Jesus as messiah or divine, and modern Jewish scholars have studied him as a Jewish teacher of the Second Temple period.
reading: Jesus was born, lived and died a Jew, and every one of his first followers was Jewish. Judaism as a religion, however, has never accepted the claims Christians make about him. In Jewish understanding, the *messiah* is a human descendant of David. He will gather the exiles, restore peace and see the world acknowledge God. None of that happened in the first century. Jewish tradition also holds that God is one and not a human being. So the Christian belief that Jesus is divine is, for Judaism, not possible. Jewish readers say this plainly, and Christian readers who study with them expect to hear it.

For most of the last two thousand years Jews said little about Jesus in writing. One reason is that Christian rulers punished what they took as insult. The Babylonian Talmud contains a few passages that some manuscripts and readers connect to Jesus. They are late, disputed and were censored in many editions. Medieval Jewish thinkers such as Maimonides, in the twelfth century, rejected Christian claims about Jesus. Maimonides also wrote that Christianity had spread knowledge of the Torah among the nations.

The modern change came with scholarship. Joseph Klausner, a professor in Jerusalem, published a Hebrew life of Jesus in 1922 that treated him as a Jewish moral teacher. Geza Vermes, a scholar at Oxford, titled his 1973 book Jesus the Jew. He set Jesus among the Galilean holy men of his day. Amy-Jill Levine, a Jewish New Testament professor in the United States, co-edited The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2011). In it Jewish scholars write notes on every book. The phrase *Second Temple Judaism* names the period from the rebuilding of the temple in 516 BCE to its destruction in 70 CE. It has become the standard frame for placing Jesus.

Dialogue has followed scholarship. Since Nostra Aetate in 1965 and parallel Protestant statements, Jewish and Christian scholars have often taught the gospels together. Chicago has seen some of this work. The 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in the city brought Jewish and Christian speakers to one platform. The city's seminaries and Jewish institutions have hosted joint study since. Jews studying Jesus as a Jewish teacher, and Christians studying him within Judaism, are two different projects. They share a great deal of ground.

words.d: in Jewish tradition, a future human king from David's line who will bring peace; Christians apply the title to Jesus
Jewish life and thought from the rebuilding of the temple in 516 BCE to its destruction in 70 CE
a twelfth-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar who wrote about Christianity's role while rejecting its claims about Jesus

look.title: Two Readers, One Title
look.text: A Jewish reader: the messiah brings the exiles home, ends war and makes God known to all. Isaiah 2:4 says nations will beat swords into plowshares. That has not happened, so the messiah has not come. A Christian reader: Jesus is the messiah, but his kingdom began in a hidden way and will be completed at his return; Isaiah 2:4 describes that completion. Both quote the same verse.
look.prompt: State each reader's argument in one sentence without using the word "wrong." What does each reader assume about how a prophecy is fulfilled?

check.q: What does Jewish tradition expect the messiah to be?
choices: A divine being who is one with God
A human king from David's line who brings peace and gathers the exiles
A prophet who will abolish the Torah
A Roman governor who converts to Judaism
check.why: In Jewish understanding the messiah is a human descendant of David whose coming brings visible peace. Jewish tradition holds that God is not a human being.

check.q: What was the title of Geza Vermes's 1973 book?
choices: The Quest of the Historical Jesus
check.why: Vermes's Jesus the Jew placed Jesus among Galilean holy men. The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2011) was co-edited by Levine, and Jesus and Judaism (1985) is by Sanders.

check.q: What period does "Second Temple Judaism" cover?
choices: From David to the Babylonian exile
From 70 CE to the completion of the Talmud
check.why: The Second Temple stood from its rebuilding in 516 BCE until Rome destroyed it in 70 CE, and Jesus lived within that period.

lessons.title: Jesus in the Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: Islam honors Jesus, called Isa, as a prophet born of the virgin Maryam who performed miracles by God's permission, but the Qur'an denies that he was God's son and, in most Muslim readings, that he was crucified.
reading: The *Qur'an* is the scripture Muslims believe God revealed to the prophet Muhammad in the seventh century. It names Jesus, in Arabic *Isa*, about twenty-five times, more often than it names Muhammad. Surah 19, named Maryam for Mary, tells of the angel's announcement and the virgin birth. The infant Jesus speaks from the cradle to defend his mother. Surah 3 and Surah 5 describe him healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead. He also shapes a bird from clay that becomes alive. Each time it is "by God's permission" (Qur'an 5:110). Mary is the only woman the Qur'an names, and she is honored above the women of the worlds (3:42).

The Qur'an also draws sharp lines. Qur'an 4:171 says Jesus was a messenger of God and God's word cast to Mary. It tells the People of the Book not to say "three," for God is one, and it is not for God to have a son. Islam's central teaching is tawhid, the oneness of God. It rules out the Christian doctrine of the Trinity and the belief that Jesus is divine. Muslims hold that Jesus, like Moses and Muhammad, brought the same message of submission to the one God. They hold that his followers later altered it.

On the crucifixion the Qur'an is brief and much discussed. Qur'an 4:157 says that those who claimed to have killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, did not kill him and did not crucify him. It was made to appear so to them. The next verse says God raised him to himself (4:158). The majority Muslim reading holds that Jesus was not crucified. Some say another person was made to resemble him; others say the event only appeared to happen. A minority of Muslim scholars read the verse as denying that his enemies truly defeated him. Many Muslims also expect Jesus to return before the Day of Judgment.

Setting the three traditions side by side gives three readings of one figure. Jews see a teacher of the Second Temple period and no messiah. Christians see the messiah, the Son of God, crucified and risen. Muslims see a great prophet, born of a virgin, not divine, not crucified, raised to God. Each tradition reads its own scripture, and each claims to describe him rightly. A public-school class describes all three accurately. It leaves the judgment where it belongs, with the reader.

words.d: the scripture of Islam, which Muslims believe God revealed to Muhammad in the seventh century; arranged in 114 surahs
the Arabic name of Jesus in the Qur'an, where he is honored as a prophet and messenger
the Islamic teaching of the absolute oneness of God, which rules out the Trinity and any divine son
the Qur'an's term for Jews and Christians, communities that received earlier scriptures

look.title: The Qur'an on the Crucifixion
look.text: The verse says that those who boasted of killing the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God, did not kill him and did not crucify him, though it was made to appear so to them; those who dispute about it are in doubt and have no sure knowledge; they did not kill him for certain. Rather, God raised him up to himself.
look.cite: Qur'an 4:157–158, paraphrased; compare the public-domain translations of Rodwell (1861) and Palmer (1880)
look.prompt: The gospels and Tacitus report a crucifixion; the Qur'an says it was made to appear so. Describe in neutral language how a Muslim reader and a Christian reader each understand the other's text.

check.q: Which surah of the Qur'an is named for Mary and tells of the birth of Jesus?
check.why: Surah 19, Maryam, recounts the annunciation and the virgin birth. Mary is the only woman the Qur'an names.

check.q: What does Qur'an 4:171 tell the People of the Book not to say?
choices: "Three," because God is one and does not have a son
check.why: The verse affirms Jesus as messenger and word of God but forbids saying "three" and denies that God has a son, in keeping with tawhid.

check.q: What is the majority Muslim reading of Qur'an 4:157 on the crucifixion?
choices: Jesus was crucified and died, as the gospels say
Jesus was not crucified; it was made to appear so, and God raised him
Jesus was crucified but did not die on the cross
The verse does not mention the crucifixion
check.why: Most Muslim interpreters hold that Jesus was not crucified and that God raised him to himself. A minority read the verse differently, but all read it as denying his enemies' victory.

lessons.title: Believing a Text and Studying It
lessons.mainIdea: A person can read the gospels as scripture, as history, or as literature, and a public school teaches the second and third while respecting the first.
reading: Three students read Mark 16:8 together. One is a Christian who believes the tomb was empty because Jesus rose; for her the verse is a doorway to Easter. One is Jewish and reads it as a text from another tradition, interesting and important, but not her scripture. One has no religion and reads it as a first-century Greek narrative that stops strangely. All three can answer the same questions: which manuscripts end here, what the women were told, how Matthew changed the scene. Their answers to those questions will match. Their answers to "is it true?" will not, and the class is not where that question gets settled.

This is the distinction between *devotional reading* and *academic study*. Devotional reading asks what the text means for me and my community, and it takes place in churches, synagogues, mosques and homes. Academic study asks what the text says, how it was made, how it has been read, and what can be known about its world. The two are not enemies. Many scholars are believers; many believers read critically. But they are different activities with different rules, and a public school does only the second.

The law in the United States draws exactly this line. In Abington School District v. Schempp (1963), the Supreme Court ruled that required Bible reading as a devotional exercise in public schools violated the First Amendment. The same opinion said that study of the Bible for its literary and historic qualities, presented objectively as part of a secular program of education, is consistent with the Constitution. This course exists because of that second sentence. It teaches about the Bible; it does not teach the Bible as true or as false.

The skill this unit has practiced is the skill the Court described. Lay the accounts side by side. Name the writer, the date, the manuscript, the reader. Attribute each belief to those who hold it: Christians believe, Jewish tradition holds, Muslims read, most historians think. Say what the text does and what it has meant. A student who can do that with the Passion narratives, the most contested chapters in the New Testament, can do it with any text she meets.

words.d: reading a text as scripture, for what it means to the reader's own faith and community
reading a text for what it says, how it was made, how it has been read and what can be known about its world
the 1963 Supreme Court case that ended devotional Bible reading in public schools and allowed objective study of the Bible

look.title: Which Kind of Question?
look.text: Sort these questions: (1) Which is the oldest manuscript of Mark? (2) Did Jesus rise from the dead? (3) How does Luke's account of the tomb differ from John's? (4) What should I believe about the resurrection? (5) When did Tacitus write the Annals? (6) Why do Muslims read the crucifixion differently from Christians?
look.prompt: Which questions belong in a public-school class and which belong to a person's own faith or conscience? For the ones that belong in class, what kind of evidence answers them?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court say in Abington v. Schempp (1963) about studying the Bible in public schools?
choices: All Bible study in public schools is forbidden
Public schools must lead daily Bible readings
Objective study of the Bible's literary and historic qualities is permitted; devotional exercises are not
Only the New Testament may be studied
check.why: The Court ended required devotional reading but stated that objective study as part of a secular education is consistent with the First Amendment.

check.q: Which of these is an academic question rather than a devotional one?
choices: How did Matthew change Mark's account of the tomb?
What does Easter mean for my life?
check.why: Comparing Matthew and Mark asks what the texts say and how one edited the other. The other three ask what the reader should believe.

check.q: What does it mean to attribute a belief?
choices: To prove that the belief is correct
To translate the belief into Greek
To remove the belief from the text
To say which tradition or reader holds the belief
check.why: Attributing means naming who holds a view: Christians believe, Jewish tradition holds, Muslims read. It neither proves nor removes the belief.

review.q: Which gospel places a long conversation between Jesus and Pilate ending with "What is truth?"
review.why: John 18:33–38 has the extended exchange. The Synoptic Pilate scenes are shorter.

review.q: About how long after the crucifixion was Mark, the earliest gospel, written according to most scholars?
review.why: Most scholars date Mark to about 70 CE, roughly forty years after a crucifixion around 30 CE.

review.q: Which detail appears in Matthew's Passion narrative only?
review.why: Only Matthew 27:24 has Pilate wash his hands. Herod is Luke's, the Kidron is John's, and the cry is in Mark and Matthew.

review.q: Why do most modern Bibles mark off Mark 16:9–20?
choices: Because it is written in Aramaic
Because the oldest manuscripts end Mark at 16:8
Because the Council of Nicaea removed it
review.why: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8; the longer ending is widely thought to be a second-century addition.

review.q: What is the earliest surviving written account of resurrection appearances?
review.why: 1 Corinthians is dated about 54 CE, earlier than any gospel. Josephus does not describe appearances.

review.q: Which two non-Christian writers mention Jesus within about ninety years of his death?
review.why: Josephus (c. 93 CE) and Tacitus (c. 116 CE) both mention him. The others lived before Jesus or did not write about him.

review.q: How does the Qur'an describe Jesus?
choices: As the Son of God who died on the cross
As a prophet born of the virgin Mary, not divine, and not crucified in most Muslim readings
As a teacher who is never named
review.why: The Qur'an honors Isa as a prophet and messenger born of Maryam, denies he is God's son (4:171), and says he was not crucified (4:157).

review.q: Which of these is a criterion historians use to weigh gospel traditions?
choices: Presence in the King James Version
review.why: Multiple attestation, along with embarrassment, dissimilarity and coherence, is a standard criterion. Popularity, length and translation are not.
